Organocatalytic Access to C1-Functionalized Indolizines via  
Remote Stereocontrolled Construction of Axially Chiral Allenes 
Xuan Zhang,a Xu-Hua Jiang,a Chun-Dong Huang,b Cheng Gao,a Shao-Fei Ni,*,b,c and Qi-Jian Ni*,a 
a College of Chemistry and Materials Science, Key Laboratory of Functionalized Molecular Solids, Ministry of Education,

Comprehensive Summary  
 
We present here a straightforward protocol for the enantioselective synthesis of axially chiral tetrasubstituted allenes enabled by chi-
ral phosphoric acid (CPA)-catalyzed 1,8-addition of indolizines to p ropargylic alcohols. This strategy achieves enantioselective and re-
gioselective C1-functionalization of indolizines under mild reaction conditions with low catalyst loading, broad functional group toler-
ance (35 examples), and excellent enantioselectivities (up to 9 6% ee). Moreover, the scale -up reac tion and late-stage C3-function-
alizations demonstrated its potential applications. DFT calculations were carried out to clarify the  reaction mechanism and the origin 
of enantio- and regioselective control.

Background and Originality Content 
Axially chiral allenes are important structural motifs common-
ly found in natural products, [1] pharmaceuticals,[2] and chiral cata-
lysts or ligands (Figure 1a). [3] Consequently, numerous methods 
for the catalytic asymme tric synthesis of chiral allenes have been 
developed,[4] primarily including direct functionalization of al -
lenes,[5] conversion of prochiral 1,3 -enyne,[6] and isomerization of 
alkynes.[7] However, most of the established approaches focus on 
synthesizing 1,3-di- or trisubstituted chiral allenes. Very recently, 
organocatalytic 1,6 -[8] or 1,8 -conjugate addition [9] of propargylic 
alcohol has been demonstrated as a powerful method for the 
construction of chiral tetrasubstituted allenes . Despite these ad -
vances, driven by the persistent challenges in accessing chiral 
tetrasubstituted allenes formation, the development of new cata -
lytic enantioselective approaches is still highly valuable and de -
sirable. 
 
Figure 1  Representative examples of functional molecules containing chiral allene 
and indolizine moiety. 
On the other hand, indolizines have garnered increasing at -
tention due to their distinctive structural features and unique 
properties, which render them highly promising for biomedical 
and fluorescence applications (Figure 1b).[10] As a result, extensive 
efforts have been devoted to synthesizing structurally diverse 
indolizines over the past decades. [11] In recent years, the direct 
functionalization of indolizines has emerged as an efficient syn -
thetic route for modifying indolizine moieties and attracted con -
siderable attention. Among these, several attractive C3 -function-
alizations of indolizines have been reported in this field, including 
C‒H activation, [12] propargylation,[13] Lewis acid catalysis, [14] visi-
ble-light or electro-induced,[15] as well as organocatalytic 1,4 -con-
jugate addition (Scheme 1a). [16] In sharp contrast to the well -de-
veloped C3-functionalization of indolizine, the direct and regiose -
lective C1-functionalization of indolizine remains challenging and 
elusive, especially for the C3 -unsubstituted derivatives. Very  
Scheme 1  Catalytic enantioselective functionalization of indolizines 
 
recently, only very few reports concerned on the regioselective 
and enantioselective C1 -functionalizations of indolizines through 
Mannich reaction.[17] Our group also successfully disclosed a CPA - 
catalyzed regio- and enantioselective C1 -arylation of β,γ-alkynyl- 
α-imino esters with pyrrolo[2,1 -a]isoquinolines.[18] Building upon 
these results, we became interested in this promising asymmetric 
C1-functionalization of indolizine via remote 1,8 -conjugate addi-
tion of in situ  generated propargylic para-quinone methides, 
providing an organocatalytic protocol for the construction of axi -
ally chiral tetrasubstituted allenes. Toward this goal,  several chal-
lenging issues should be concerned: 1) controlling nucleophilic 
attack by indolizines at C1 versus C3-position; 2) achieving site - 
selective 1,6- or 1,8 -conjugate addition of propargylic -para-qui-
none methides; 3) establishing remote stereocontrol from the 
reaction site without hydrogen bonding involvement. 
Results and Discussion 
To achieve this transformation, we initiated our investigation 
by selecting racemic propargylic alcohol 1a and indolizine 2a as 
the model substrates  (Table 1). The initial test was performed in 
the presence of 10 mol% CPA catalyst C1 at room temperature. To 
our delight, the desired chiral a llene 3aa was obtained in 46% 
yield with 50% ee and the regioisomeric C3 -adduct 4aa was iso-
lated in 15% yield (entry 1). Notably, the absence of the 1,6 -ad-
dition adduct confirmed the exclusive 1,8 -site specificity of this 
approach. Decreasing the reactio n temperature to ‒40 °C im-
proved the ee value to 75% while maintaining a comparable yield 
upon extended reaction time  (entry 2). To further enhance the 
enantio- and regioselectivity, some other catalysts with different 
substituents and scaffolds were then evaluated, and catalyst C2, 
possessing bulkier 2,4,6 -tricyclohexylphenyl substituents at the

ing results, we screened various mixed solvents. No superior al -
ternatives were identified when mixing DCM with other solvents, 
such as toluene, CCl 4, CHCl3, or n-hexane (entries 6‒9). Subse-
quently, catalyst loading was investigated due to the high reactiv -
ity (entries 10‒12). Notably, the enantio - and regioselectivity  of 
chiral allene  3aa were well maintained with only 1 mol% of C2 
upon extended reaction time  (18 h, entry 12) . Control experi -
ments confirmed that no reaction occurred in the absence of cat -
alyst. 
With the optimal reaction conditions established, we next ex-
plored the scope and generality of the reaction. As summarized in 
Scheme 2 , this 1,8-addition proceeded efficiently with a wide 
range of propargylic alcohols 1. Various substituents on the phe-
nyl-tethered alkyne  (R1) were well tolerated, affording the C1 - 
selective 1,8-adducts 3aa‒3ma in moderate to good yields, excel -
lent enantioselectivities and regioselective ratios  (rr) of 2  : 1 to 5  : 
1. T he electronic nature and the position of  the substituents on  
the aromatic R 1 moiety did not significantly affect  the formation 
of tetrasubstituted chiral allenes. Furthermore, naphthyl and  het-
erocyclic substituents  also reacted smoothly with indolizine 2a, 
producing the corresponding 3na‒3qa in moderate yields, ac-
ceptable rr and 87%‒95% ee. In addition, alkyl (R1 = n-Bu) substi-
tuted propargylic alcohols  furnished the chiral allene 3ra in 37% 
yield with 93% ee and 2  : 1 rr . Remarkably, the more challenging 
bulky t-butyl group on the alkyne was compatible, delivering 3ra 
with only a slight decrease in enantioselectivity. The propargylic 
aryl ring (R2) was also amenable to this transformation. Both elec-
tron-donating (Me or MeO) and electron -withdrawing (F or Cl) 
substituents on the phenyl ring of R 2 were compatible and gave 
the corresponding chiral alle nes 3ta‒3wa in 53%‒72% yields, 
81%‒91% ee and rr of 3 : 1‒4 : 1.

The scope of the indolizines was then evaluated by the 1,8-ad-
dition with propargylic  alcohols 1a (Scheme 3). Variations on the 
ester moiety at the C2 position of indolizine were well tolerated 
under the optimal conditions and furnished the desired 3ab‒3ad 
in moderate yields with exc ellent enantioselectivities (91%‒93% 
ee) and good regioselective ratios (rr 3  : 1‒4 : 1). Substituents on 
the indolizine ring were also investigated.  As expected, t he reac-
tion with indolizines bearing substituents at C 5 position blocked 
the 1,8-addition at C3 site, thus affording adducts 3ae and 3af in 
excellent regioselectivities, good yields and 87%‒91% ee. Fur-
thermore, both electron-donating and electron-withdrawing 
groups at C6 and C7 positions of indolizines proceeded smoothly 
to produce 3ag‒3ak in 45%‒73% yields with 85%‒96% ee. In ad -
dition, 8 -methylindolizine proved a suitable substrate, affording 
3al in 45% yield with 95% ee and 1  : 1 rr . Significantly, extension of 
this protocol to the pyrroloquinoline ring successful ly produced 
the expected 3am in 62% yield with excellent enantio - and regi-
oselectivity (88% ee, 4  : 1 rr), demonstrating broad compatibility 
of our methodology.

In order to demonstrate the synthetic utility of this protocol, 
scale-up preparation and product derivatization were conducted 
(Scheme 4). A scale -up reaction between racemic 1h and 2a pro-
ceeded smoothly, giving product 3ha in 73% yield with 93% ee  
and 3.5 : 1 rr. To further showcase the synthetic value of this work, 
we first protected the hydroxy group via a one-pot reaction with 
TsCl, yielding sulfonate 5ha in 72% yield and 90% ee. Notably, the 
unsubstituted C3 -position provided great potential fo r further 
functionalization. For example, the direct C ‒H amination of 5ha 
with azodicarboxylate proceeded smoothly to yield product 6ha 
in 70% yield with 89% ee.  In addition, subjecting C3 -substituted 
indolizine 2n to the one-pot reaction also delivered su lfonate 5an 
in 72% yield and 69% ee. The structure of product 5an was eluci-
dated by X -ray crystallographic analysis, and the absolute config -
uration of product 5ha was unambiguously assigned by compari -
son between its experimental and calculated electronic circular 
dichroism spectra, which was conf irmed to be the ( S) configura-
tion (for details, see the SI).

tion of the indolizine 2p resulted in only 9% conversion with 40% 
ee value of 3ap, indicating a detrimental H -bond interaction be -
tween the indolizine and the CPA catalyst (Scheme 5a). Further -

the reaction with indolizine 2a under the standard conditions. The 
reaction proceeded smoothly , affording 3aa with comparable 
results (Scheme 5b). This observation in combination with the 
control experiment that no reaction occurred between methylat-
ed propargylic alcohol 1a’ and indolizine 2a under the standard 
reaction conditions demonstrated that 1,8-addition was the rate- 
and enantio-determining step and ruled out an ion-pairing activa-
tion mode. The kinetic studies as shown in Scheme 5e indicated 
that ee value of the product remained constant  (93% ee)  and 
substrate 1a remained racemic throughout the reaction progress . 
These results, combined with the related reports, implied the 
enantioselective outcome relied entirely on the CPA catalyst via a 
dynamic kinetic resolution during the catalytic process .[9a-b] In 
addition, several control 31P NMR experiments disclosed the weak 
interaction of CPA catalyst with p ropargylic alcohol 1a and in -
dolizine 2a (Scheme 5d). Interestingly, the reaction performed at   
‒40 °C in the presence of catalyst  C2 delivered C1-functionalized 
3aa in 93% ee with 5  : 1 rr . Upon warming the mixture to room 
temperature, the 3aa : 4aa ratio dropped to an equilibrium value 
of 1  : 1 (Scheme 5c). This finding establishes 3aa as the kinetically 
controlled C1 -regioisomer, whereas elevated temperatures drive 
equilibration toward the thermodynamically favored C3 -regioiso-
mer 4aa. Finally, the observed linear proportionality between the 
ee values of product 3aa and catalyst C2 (Scheme 5f) strongly 
supported a monomolecular catalyst involvement in the enantio -
determining 1,8-addition transition state. 
To gain deeper mechanistic insights, density functional theory 
(DFT) calculations were systematically performed. The reaction 
pathway begins with the dehydration of substrate 1a catalyzed by 
chiral phosphonic acid (CPA), leading to the formation of key in -
termediate I1. Su bsequently, substrate 2a approaches I1 under 
the stereocontrol of CPA, where two competitive pathways 
emerge:  (1) the kinetically favored 1,8 -addition proceeding 
through transition state TS1 with a Gibbs free energy barrier of 
15.1 kcal/mol to afford produ ct 3aa; and (2) the thermodynami -
cally controlled 1,6-addition via transition state TS1' with a higher 
barrier of 18.5 kcal/mol, yielding regioisomer 4aa. Notably, an 
enantioselective 1,8-addition pathway was also identified, exhib -
iting an energy barrier of 18.5 kcal/mol for TS1''. Both side reac -
tions demonstrate a significant 3.4 kcal/mol higher energy barrier 
compared to the main 1,8 -addition pathway, rationalizing the 
observed kinetic preference for 3aa formation. To further analyze 
the mechanism, density functional theory (DFT) calculations were  
carried out. Initially, substrate 1a was dehydrated with the chiral 
phosphonic acid catalyst CPA, resulting in the formation of inter -

reaction occurs, producing the thermodynamically controlled

To elucidate the origin of regioselectivity  and enantioselectiv-
ity in the reaction, three distinct transition states ( TS1, TS1' and 
TS1'', Figure 2) were identified, respectively forming the main 
product, regioselective product and enantiomeric product. For 
regioselectivity, energy decomposition a nalysis revealed that the 
energy difference between TS1 and TS1' primarily originates from 
differential catalyst -substrate interactions. Detailed structural 
analysis demonstrated significant differences in non -covalent 
interactions: TS1 features multiple stabilizing C–H···O interactions 
(b1 = 2.122 Å, b2 = 2.071 Å, b3 = 2.328 Å) and π–π interaction (b4 
= 3.183 Å) between the catalyst and substrate fragment, while 
TS1' possesses only one C –H···O interaction (b5 = 1.849 Å) and 
one π–π interaction (b6 = 3.258 Å). This disparity in stabilizing 
interactions accounts for the relative preference for TS1. All these 
interactions could be visualized from NCI plot (see details in Sup -

Conclusions 
In conclusion, we have successfully established a CPA -cata-
lyzed 1,8-conjugate addition of propargylic alcoho ls with indoliz -
ines, enabling direct access to axially chiral tetrasubstituted al -
lenes via remote stereocontrolled C1 -functionalization. This 
strategy addresses the long -standing challenge of regioselective 
C1-attack on indolizines, featuring  mild condit ions, low catalyst 
loading, broad substrate scope with high regio- and enantiocon-
trol. The reaction scalability and late -stage derivatization demon-
strated their potential as versatile chiral building blocks. Mecha -
nistic studies and DFT calculations conf irm a kinetically favored 
C1-attack pathway, providing insights for future asymmetric de -
sign. 
Experimental 
General experimental procedures : To a 4 mL vial was added 
propargyl alcohol 1 (0.1 mmol, 1.0 equiv), indolizine 2 (0.12 mmol, 
1.2 equiv) and (R)-C2 (0.001 mmol, 1 mol%) in DCE  : c-hexane = 4 : 
1 (1 mL, V/V). The mixture was stirred at ‒40 ° C and monitored by 
TLC until completion of the reaction. The reaction mixture was 
directly subjected to flash column chromatography on silica gel 
(petroleum ether/ethyl acetate 8 : 1) to afford the product 3.

Comprehensive Summary

We present here a straightforward protocol for the enantioselective synthesis of axially chiral tetrasubstituted allenes enabled by chi-
ral phosphoric acid (CPA)-catalyzed 1,8-addition of indolizines to propargylic alcohols. This strategy achieves enantioselective and re-
gioselective C1-functionalization of indolizines under mild reaction conditions with low catalyst loading, broad functional group toler-
ance (35 examples), and excellent enantioselectivities (up to 96% ee). Moreover, the scale-up reaction and late-stage C3-function-
alizations demonstrated its potential applications. DFT calculations were carried out to clarify the reaction mechanism and the origin
of enantio- and regioselective control.

lysts or ligands (Figure 1a).<sup>[3]</sup> Consequently, numerous methods
for the catalytic asymmetric synthesis of chiral allenes have been
developed,<sup>[4]</sup> primarily including direct functionalization of al-
lenes,<sup>[5]</sup> conversion of prochiral

elusive, especially for the C3-unsubstituted derivatives. Very

To achieve this transformation, we initiated our investigation
by selecting racemic propargylic alcohol 1a and indolizine 2a as
the model substrates (Table 1). The initial test was performed in
the presence of 10 mol% CPA catalyst C1 at room temperature. To
our delight, the desired chiral allene 3aa was obtained in 46%
yield with 50% ee and the regioisomeric C3-adduct 4aa was iso-
lated in 15% yield (entry 1). Notably, the absence of the 1,6-ad-
dition adduct confirmed the exclusive 1,8-site specificity of this
approach. Decreasing the reaction temperature to ‒40 °C im-
proved the ee value to 75% while maintaining a comparable yield
upon extended reaction time (entry 2). To further enhance the
enantio- and regioselectivity, some other catalysts with different
substituents and scaffolds were then evaluated, and catalyst C2,
possessing bulkier 2,4,6-tricyclohexylphenyl substituents at the

with only a slight decrease in enantioselectivity. The propargylic

Conclusions

In conclusion, we have successfully established a CPA-cata-
lyzed 1,8-conjugate addition of propargylic alcohols with indoliz-
ines, enabling direct access to axially chiral tetrasubstituted al-
lenes via remote stereocontrolled C1-functionalization. This
strategy addresses the long-standing challenge of regioselective
C1-attack on indolizines, featuring mild conditions, low catalyst
loading, broad substrate scope with high regio- and enantiocon-
trol. The reaction scalability and late-stage derivatization demon-
strated their potential as versatile chiral building blocks. Mecha-
nistic studies and DFT calculations confirm a kinetically favored
C1-attack pathway, providing insights for future asymmetric de-
sign.
